source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat undergraduates on a text matrix task built from Raven rules, zero-shot. Its error pattern by problem type resembled human patterns.
numbers: Digit Matrices: humans N=40. GPT-3 vs humans, generative answers OR=1.88 (95% CI 1.21-2.91, p=0.005); multiple choice OR=6.27 (CI 3.28-11.99). Item-pattern correlation with humans r(30)=0.39, p=0.027. Best human got every item right.
limits: Materials may overlap training data (disputed in c03, c05). Rule induction and filling a cell, not explicit transfer of surmises from base to target.
agent_relevance: Shows a model can infer the missing piece from a relational pattern. This is the machine form of a candidate inference, but only for tidy formal tasks.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) story analogy section (Gentner et al. materials)
finding: On stories where only the causal (higher-order) relations match, college students clearly beat GPT-3. GPT-4 did better in a preliminary test.
numbers: Humans N=54; 15/54 chose the analogous story on every trial. Pooled near+far: GPT-3 binomial p=0.0005, humans t(53)=21.3. Near: GPT-3 p=0.0039. Far (cross-domain): GPT-3 p=0.065 (not significant), humans t(53)=16.7. GPT-3 vs humans OR=0.37, p=0.0003.
limits: GPT-4 result is a supplementary check, not a full study. Two-choice task, chance 50%.
agent_relevance: Systematicity (causal structure) is where the model is weakest; a candidate inference that rests on a causal chain from a far domain is the case most likely to be unsound.

source: Hodel & West (2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Reply to Webb et al. Argues the problems may sit in training data, and that GPT-3 fails on simple variants while humans stay high.
numbers: With a synthetic alphabet, GPT-3 generative accuracy was below 0.1 on extend-sequence, successor/predecessor and fix-alphabet variants. Only remove-redundant-letter and sort stayed near the original range. Human accuracy stayed similar across modifications.
limits: GPT-3 only. Webb et al. reply (c05) shows a counting bottleneck explains part of the drop.
agent_relevance: Warns that tests that look like transfer may be recall of seen patterns. Our O7 must test the transferred step on the real target, not trust that it looks right.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: On letter-string analogies with permuted or non-letter alphabets, human accuracy stays high while GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 drop sharply. Models and humans make different kinds of errors.
numbers: Error table (percent of errors, as printed; row labels in the PDF text layer are partly garbled): GPT-3 5.81 / 30.97 / 55.48 / 7.74; GPT-4 22.00 / 32.67 / 42.67 / 2.67; humans 38.59 / 14.67 / 34.24 / 12.50 across alternative-rule / incorrect-rule / wrong / completely-wrong. Humans find a valid alternative rule far more often.
limits: Humans tested on Prolific with the original 14-problem set; models given the Hodel and West prompt. Counting bottleneck is a competing explanation (c05).
agent_relevance: Humans reinterpret and find a valid alternative rule when the first mapping fails. A step-transfer test should invite the agent to look for an alternative rule.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: GPT-4 with code execution solved the permuted-alphabet letter-string problems at about human level, without being told to use code. The earlier failures were partly a counting problem.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). GPT-4 with code execution vs humans: no significant difference (P=0.496); GPT-4 without code was significantly worse. 46% of GPT-4 errors used a valid alternative rule vs 39% of human errors in Lewis and Mitchell.
quote: GPT-4 was able to solve these counterfactual letter-string analogies at a roughly human level of performance when given the ability to count using code execution
limits: Authors' own rebuttal, not independent. Only one counterfactual family tested.
agent_relevance: A tool (code) rescues the exact step where the model fails. Supports checking transferred steps by executing them, not by judging them.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024/25) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Extends the robustness test to digit matrices and story analogies. Brittle on most variants. On stories, models are hurt by answer order and by paraphrase more than humans.
numbers: Letter strings: GPT drops sharply while humans stay high on two variant types. Digit matrices: drop on only one of two variant types. Stories: GPT sensitive to answer-order effects; more sensitive to paraphrase than humans. (Exact per-model numbers not extracted this session.)
limits: Older GPT versions; complexity washes out differences when all do badly.
agent_relevance: Order and wording of options change what the model infers. Shuffle and rephrase candidate inferences before trusting any one verdict.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning, J. Memory and Language 145
finding: New task mapping words to abstract symbol sequences. Best LLMs match humans in the default condition but differ on presentation changes and distractors.
numbers: Defaults: GPT-4, Claude 3, Llama-405B not significantly worse than humans (p=0.097, 0.194, 0.097). Small models: Pythia-12B 0.0, Falcon-40B 0.1, GPT-3 0.5, Claude 2 0.6 match to reference. Permuted Pairs: LLMs drop (Claude 3 coef -1.78, GPT-4 -1.68, Llama -2.34, all p<0.001), humans do not. Distracted: all four fall about 0.25. Temperature 0.7.
limits: Single university sample, student selection effect noted by authors. Match to reference, not true accuracy.
agent_relevance: The inference the mapping sanctions is applied to a new string. Models do this about as well as people when the order is clean and worse when it is shuffled.

source: Musker et al. (2025) Only-RHS and Random Finals conditions
finding: Humans drop the useless left-hand side when it is clearly random; models do not. Models over-trust a misleading source.
numbers: Only RHS: GPT-4 0.9 (not different from humans, p=0.824), Claude 3 about 0.8 (p=0.046), Llama-405B about 0.5 (p<0.001). Random Finals: humans fall about 0.5; Claude 3 falls 0.5, GPT-4 0.8, Llama 0.4.
limits: Mechanism is inferred from behaviour only.
agent_relevance: A bad source analog can pull the model into a wrong inference even when the target alone suffices. Keep a no-analogy baseline in O7 and compare.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Telling the model to recall relevant solved problems before solving (self-generated exemplars) beat 0-shot CoT and 5-shot CoT on several tasks. This is the first AI-agent form of retrieve-then-transfer.
numbers: Table 1 (read from table text, row order 0-shot, 0-shot CoT, 5-shot CoT, Ours): GSM8K GPT-3.5-turbo 76.7 vs 77.8; PaLM2 80.7 vs 81.7; davinci-003 54.0 vs 61.0. MATH GPT-3.5 34.9 vs 37.3; PaLM2 34.3 vs 34.8.
limits: Gains are small on strong models (about 1 point GSM8K). Table text layer is hard to align, so check against the paper before quoting.
agent_relevance: Direct template for O7: ask for related solved cases first. But see c12-c13: the benefit may not come from relevance.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) scale and exemplar count ablations
finding: Self-generated analogies only help when the model is big enough. Small models do better with retrieved labelled examples.
numbers: text-curie-001 and davinci-001: few-shot CoT beats self-generation; davinci-002/003: self-generation wins. K=1 exemplar hurts (GSM8K 76.1, MATH 34.8); K=3 to 5 best (GSM8K 77.5-77.8, MATH 37.0-37.3), GPT-3.5-turbo.
limits: Old model family.
agent_relevance: Candidate-inference quality depends on the model's own knowledge. Single analog is risky: use three or more.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Codeforces results
finding: Adding self-generated knowledge plus exemplars gave the biggest gain on code contests.
numbers: 3-shot CoT: GPT-3.5-turbo-16k Acc@1 13%, Acc@10 25%; GPT-4 17% and 32%. Ours knowledge+exemplars: 15% and 29% (GPT-3.5), 19% and 37% (GPT-4). With it, GPT-3.5 at 15% Acc@1 nears GPT-4's 16% baseline.
limits: Small absolute numbers; no confidence intervals reported.
agent_relevance: Writing down the transferable principle (knowledge) before the examples adds value for hard tasks.

source: Qin et al. (2025) Relevant or random: can LLMs truly perform analogical reasoning?
finding: Failed replication of the relevance story on maths. Self-generated irrelevant or random examples did as well or better than relevant ones.
numbers: GPT-3.5, 500 test items per set, 3 seeds. GSM8K/MATH: relevant 71.5/33.3 (avg 52.4); no-type 75.5/36.1 (55.8); random-same-domain 75.1/36.3; random-different 76.3/34.1; random-biology 75.3/34.6. BBH average: relevant 63.2 vs 61.9 no-type (+1.3).
limits: Relevance helps a little on BBH only. Mostly GPT-3.5 plus GPT-4o-mini checks.
agent_relevance: The gain from analogical prompting is probably not from analogy. Do not claim O7 works because of analogy until a no-analogy control is run.

source: Qin et al. (2025) accuracy of the generated examples is the key factor
finding: Relevant self-generated examples were less accurate. Raising example accuracy raised scores; wrong examples lowered them.
numbers: MATH example accuracy: relevant 62.0%, no-type 72.0%, random-same 86.0%. GPT-4-corrected examples beat uncorrected ones in every cell; random answers always worst. Two cheaper methods (generate a fixed set once, verify it) matched or beat the original at lower cost: ICL-math avg 56.3, ICL-bio 56.4 vs relevant 52.4.
limits: Mathematical tasks. Authors note answers may matter less in classification ICL.
agent_relevance: A candidate inference is only as good as the checked solution behind it. Verify the source case before transfer.

source: Yu et al. (2024, ICLR) Thought propagation
finding: Model proposes and solves analogous problems, then reuses their results to fix or replace its first answer. Gains over IO, CoT, ToT and BaG.
numbers: Shortest path, 100 problems; optimal-rate 0-shot: GPT-3.5 TP 0.65 vs IO 0.33, CoT 0.26, ToT 0.22; GPT-4 TP 0.88 vs IO 0.78; PaLM-2 TP 0.36 vs IO 0.14. Abstract: +12 points shortest path, +13% human preference in creative writing, +15% ALFWorld completion.
limits: Analogous problems here are neighbour sub-problems, closer to decomposition than far analogy. 1-layer and 2-layer TP differ little; cost rises.
agent_relevance: Closest existing agent-loop form of transfer-then-test: propagate solutions of related problems into the current one and re-evaluate.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Thought propagation on ALFWorld agents
finding: In a 134-environment text game, plans built from successful similar tasks are compared with the agent's own plan (self-evaluation or simulation). Works without a failure memory and adds on top of Reflexion-style reflection.
numbers: ALFWorld 134 environments, 6 trials to match Reflexion. Four variants TP-SE, TP-SM, TP-SR-SE, TP-SR-SM. Abstract reports +15% task completion rate. (Per-variant table values not extracted.)
limits: Claimed gain is an average across baselines.
agent_relevance: Same two-plan pick as our O7: take the transferred plan and the native plan and choose by test, not by taste.

source: Yuan et al. (2023) Beneath surface similarity: SCAR scientific analogies
finding: Asking models to abduce concept mappings between two systems (camera and eye) is hard. GPT-4 is best, below humans. A one-shot example and background help.
numbers: SCAR: 400 analogies, 13 fields. Average accuracy: GPT-4 65.0-66.2 vanilla, 68.5-69.1 with 1-shot, up to 77.17 with 1-shot plus background on one language split; ChatGPT 57.9-62.1; InstructGPT003 38.8-44.1; humans 85.9-88.5 (two undergraduates). 69.35% of ChatGPT-made mapping explanations judged accurate.
limits: Human baseline is two students. Table layout partly garbled in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Mapping quality bounds candidate-inference quality. Giving background knowledge about both systems gives the largest lift.

source: Ye, Wang, Khashabi (2024) AnaloBench
finding: Finding the matching story is hard, especially when stories are long or the bank is large. Scale helps little for long stories.
numbers: 340 human-written analogies; 12 open and 3 proprietary models. Human-GPT-4 gap 6.9 points on 1-sentence stories, 28.8 points on 30-sentence stories. Selected appendix T1 rows (1/10/30 sentence): GPT-3.5 71.8/51.2/31.5; GPT-4 55.1/27.1/20.3; Claude 65.3/46.4/30.8; human 89.1/66.5/60.7. Chance 25%.
limits: Row alignment in the appendix text is uncertain; GPT-4 may have an edge on its own extended stories (checked: little drop on Claude stories).
agent_relevance: Retrieval of a good source is the weak link at scale. Do not assume the agent will find the right analog from a long context.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: Analogical reasoning on narratives
finding: Models spot near analogies but fail far ones. Solved examples and CoT help. Even the best few-shot model is only halfway between random and human.
numbers: Humans far-analogy 94.1%. Models average 39.6% on far analogies zero-shot (below 50% chance); GPT-4 below random. Near analogies: humans 97.9%, models 75.0%.
limits: Binary task, 50% chance.
agent_relevance: Models take surface overlap as support. A candidate inference from a similar-looking story is the typical false positive.

source: Khojasteh et al. (2026) YARN: LLM abstractions plus structure mapping for narrative analogy
finding: Code does the one-to-one greedy mapping (an SME/FAME-style engine); LLM supplies the unit abstractions. Abstractions turn a below-chance mapper into a competitive one.
numbers: MCQ: mapping without abstraction 0.17 (Qwen, chance 0.25); with conceptual+evaluative abstraction 0.46 (Qwen), 0.45 (Llama, up from 0.16); best LLM-only 0.41 (Qwen), 0.28 (Llama). ARN far analogies: Llama YARN 0.46 vs LLM 0.42; Qwen zero-shot beat YARN on far (0.52 vs 0.47) and CoT beat it on near (0.79 vs 0.69).
limits: Small open models; mapping uses embedding similarity, which misses causal and negation structure.
agent_relevance: Matches our plan: LLM writes the typed relations, code maps them. Abstraction level is the main lever. Wins on far analogies for Llama, loses on near.

source: Puranam, Sen, Workiewicz (2025) Can LLMs help improve analogical reasoning for strategic decisions?
finding: GPT-4 recalls nearly every relevant analogy but applies wrong ones often. Humans apply few, but correctly. The weak point is matching (judging the structural fit), not retrieval.
numbers: Humans n=199; GPT-4 n=60 independent runs. Hint raised human analogy use: HR problem about 37% (17/46) vs 20.3% without; factory problem 8.7% (4/46) vs 6.3%. Radiation-story use without hint 6.7% (1/15). GPT-4 high recall, low precision; human recall low (e.g. 6.25%, 22%), precision near 100% in cases reported.
limits: Few observations per cell (15). Business tasks, Sept 2024 GPT-4.
agent_relevance: LLMs overgenerate candidate inferences. Add a strict filter: only keep an inference whose supporting causal link is stated and checked.

source: Hu et al. (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Putting visual Raven matrices into text (entity, layout, attribute abstractions) lets PLMs do zero-shot completion above human level on some sub-tasks. Higher-level abstraction helps more.
numbers: Abstract: zero-shot reasoning exceeds human performance and nears supervised vision methods. Text gives e.g. 77.2% (GPT-3 175B, Center) and up to 93.2% on 3x3Grid; accuracy rises with model size.
limits: Different sub-tasks reported; only selected values read.
agent_relevance: Describing the relation at the right abstraction level before inferring is what makes the inference work.

source: Shen, Druckmann, Zou (2026) Unlocking LLM creativity in science through analogical reasoning
finding: Telling the model to build a cross-domain analogy and transfer a solution gives more diverse and more novel solutions. Humans judged AR solutions more novel but less often reasonable.
numbers: Novel solutions: Claude 1.6% baseline, 21.6% cross-domain baseline, 50.4% AR; GPT 9.0%, 28.2%, 58.8%; Gemini 8.9%, 37.8%, 68.9% (as read from the paper text, model rows partly inferred). Solution diversity (Vendi) up 90-173%. Humans: AR more novel 78% of time (kappa 0.445); reasonable 67% for AR vs 86% for cross-domain baseline.
limits: Novelty judged by LLM and humans; no outcome test of transferred solutions.
agent_relevance: Transfer buys novelty at the price of validity (67% vs 86% reasonable). Test step is needed.

source: Khojasteh/Ilievski group (2026) When models know more than they say: probing analogical reasoning
finding: Reading hidden states beats prompting for rhetorical analogies in open models, but not for narrative analogies, where both are low.
numbers: Abstract plus skim: probing significantly outperforms prompting on rhetorical analogies; similar low performance on narrative analogies. (Numbers not extracted.)
limits: Open-source models only.
agent_relevance: Suggests the model sometimes holds the relation but fails to state it. A structured relation list prompt may recover some of it.

source: Chang et al. (2025) BioSpark: beyond analogical inspiration to LLM-augmented transfer
finding: A design tool that makes the model carry a mechanism from a biological source to the user's problem (Sparks cards), with trade-offs and Q&A cards. Users produced more ideas.
numbers: Abstract: workshops with professional designers and a controlled study; more generated ideas, rated higher. (Exact counts not extracted.)
limits: Human-in-the-loop tool, not an autonomous agent.
agent_relevance: Shows the pattern find, map, transfer, weigh trade-offs as a workflow, with the trade-off step explicit.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) Structure-mapping engine; candidate inference rule (background, not opened)
finding: In SME, a candidate inference is a base fact connected to matched structure but missing in the target; it is projected only if its supporting structure maps. This is the pure-code version of what the LLM studies above do by prompt.
numbers: No numbers this session.
limits: Not opened. Cited from memory of the SME literature; verify before quoting.
agent_relevance: Run SME-style projection in code on typed relations; ask the LLM only to extract relations and to judge the projected surmise.

source: Gap note: direct tests of candidate-inference projection by LLMs (searched, none found)
finding: Web search quota ran out. Using arXiv listing search by title, no paper was found that measures projection of unmatched base facts into a target as a separate LLM task. Nearest are c06, c12, c17, c19.
numbers: none
limits: Search was limited to arXiv title lists; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors.
agent_relevance: Treat our O7 test (transfer, then check on the target) as untested ground; build a small eval.
